items.stem: A company runs an order-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The application reads and writes objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. Company policy requires that no long-term credentials are stored where the application runs. The company also runs a private certificate authority that issues certificates to its servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region

options.text: Attach an IAM role through an instance profile, and let the AWS SDK load the temporary credentials from the instance metadata.
options.why: The instance profile passes the role to the instances, and code can [get automatic temporary security credentials from the instance metadata](../facts/iam.md#iam-instance-profile-one-role-and-metadata-credentials), so no key is stored.

options.text: Use IAM Roles Anywhere with certificates from the private certificate authority, and exchange each certificate for temporary role credentials.
options.why: It works, but it [requires PKI, the ability to issue and manage certificates](../facts/iam.md#iam-roles-anywhere-for-on-premises-and-hybrid-workloads), for instances that already get role credentials from AWS.
options.misconception: uses the method for servers outside AWS on EC2 instances

options.text: Create an IAM user for the application, store its access key in an encrypted file where the application runs, and rotate it monthly.
options.why: Access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), so a stored key breaks the company policy, even when it is encrypted.

options.text: Move the application to new Amazon EC2 instances, and attach an IAM role to the new instances through an instance profile.
options.why: The application already runs on EC2, so a role on the current instances does the same job without a migration.
options.misconception: moves a workload to solve a credentials problem

items.explanation: The application runs on EC2, so the shortest path is a role. [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed), and the credentials are [temporary and updated automatically](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically). Nothing is stored, and no key needs rotation by hand.
items.takeaway: Code on EC2 gets credentials from an instance profile role, not from a stored key.
items.twin: If the stem said "servers in the company's data center" instead: IAM Roles Anywhere, because it [extends the capabilities of IAM to on-premises and hybrid cloud workloads](../facts/iam.md#iam-roles-anywhere-for-on-premises-and-hybrid-workloads).
items.say: On EC2 I'd attach a role through an instance profile, so no key is stored.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the application runs on Amazon EC2 instances, no long-term credentials can be stored where it runs, and a private certificate authority exists.
Before I look at the options, I predict an IAM role through an instance profile, because AWS delivers the temporary credentials of a role to an EC2 instance.
I remove the IAM user, because its access key stays valid until someone revokes it. I remove the move to new instances, because the application already runs on EC2.

Between the instance profile and IAM Roles Anywhere the difference is where the code runs; the stem says EC2 instances, so the certificate authority is bait, and Roles Anywhere would only add certificates to manage.
Check: the instance profile meets every constraint, stores no key and needs no certificates. Time: 90 seconds.

items.stem: A company has an IAM role in its production account for reading reports from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same account. Developers in the company's development account must use the role. Their IAM policies allow sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN. When a developer calls AssumeRole, the call fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the call fails with an access denied error

options.text: Update the trust policy of the role in the production account so that it names the development account as a principal.
options.why: The AssumeRole call itself fails, and the caller side already allows it. The trust policy [names who can assume the role](../facts/iam.md#iam-role-trust-policy-names-who-can-assume).

options.text: Update the permissions policy of the role so that it allows s3:GetObject on the report bucket and on the objects in it.
options.why: The permissions policy acts after the session exists, and here the AssumeRole call itself fails, so the trust side is broken.
options.misconception: fixes the permissions side when the trust check fails

options.text: Add a bucket policy to the report bucket that allows s3:GetObject for the development account as the principal.
options.why: It does not touch the failing AssumeRole call, and across accounts AWS [allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies).

options.text: Create an IAM user in the production account for each developer, with an access key and read access to the bucket.
options.why: It works, but each user brings long-term keys that [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), which is more work and more risk.
options.misconception: replaces a role with long-term keys

items.explanation: A role has two policies. The trust policy [names who can assume the role](../facts/iam.md#iam-role-trust-policy-names-who-can-assume), and the permissions policy decides what the session can do. The developers' own allow for sts:AssumeRole is [only half of the cross-account trust](../facts/iam.md#iam-assume-role-two-permissions-checked). The call still fails, so the trust policy lacks the development account.
items.takeaway: AssumeRole fails: check the trust policy and the caller's own allow. A later call fails: fix the permissions policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "the call succeeds, but the next call to read a report fails" instead: update the permissions policy, because the trust check already passed.
items.say: AssumeRole itself fails, and their side allows it, so the trust policy is missing the development account.

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The company adds new member accounts every month. Administrators in each member account can edit the IAM policies of that account. The security team must ensure that no principal in any member account, including the root user, can stop or delete the AWS CloudTrail trail of the account. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: adds new member accounts every month

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the actions that stop or delete CloudTrail trails, and attach the SCP to the root of the organization.
options.why: Attached [to the root of your organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-attach-at-root-ou-or-account), the SCP reaches every member account, new ones too, and it applies [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the actions that stop or delete CloudTrail trails, and attach it to each member account when the account is created.
options.why: It works, but every new account needs one more attachment, which is more work than one SCP on the root of the organization.
options.misconception: attaches an organization guardrail account by account

options.text: Remove the actions that stop or delete CloudTrail trails from the identity-based policies of every IAM user and IAM role in the member accounts.
options.why: Administrators can add the actions back, and you [cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-root-user-no-identity-policies-or-boundary).
options.misconception: believes that removing an allow inside an account stops the administrators of that account

options.text: Set a permissions boundary that leaves out the actions that stop or delete CloudTrail trails on every IAM user and IAM role.
options.why: A boundary does not reach the root user, because you [cannot set a permissions boundary for the root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-root-user-no-identity-policies-or-boundary).

items.explanation: The stem asks for a guardrail that holds against administrators and the root user. Member account principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps), and an SCP limits principals [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user). Its Deny wins, because [an explicit deny overrides an explicit allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-explicit-deny-overrides-allow).
items.takeaway: To stop everyone in member accounts, the root user too, put a Deny in an SCP on the organization root.
items.twin: If the stem said "the trail of the management account" instead: an SCP does not help, because SCPs [do not affect users or roles in the management account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-no-effect-on-management-account).
items.say: A Deny in an SCP sits above every member account, so administrators and the root user lose the action.

items.stem: A company has two AWS accounts. An application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in account A and uses an IAM role. The application must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket in account B. The security team requires that the bucket stays private and that access is limited to this one application. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements MOST securely? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy in account B that allows s3:GetObject for the ARN of the application's IAM role in account A.
options.why: The [resource-based policy in the trusting account must allow the requester](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies), and this statement names one role.

options.text: Add a statement to the identity-based policy of the IAM role in account A that allows s3:GetObject on the objects in the bucket.
options.why: The [identity-based policy in the trusted account must allow the access](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies), so account A grants the action too.

options.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy in account B that allows s3:GetObject with the wildcard character as the principal of the statement.
options.why: A wildcard principal with Allow grants access to all users, [including anonymous users (public access)](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-wildcard-is-public), so the bucket is no longer private.

options.text: Create an IAM user in account B with read access to the bucket, and store the access key of the user on the EC2 instances.
options.why: It works, but stored access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), which is less secure than a role.

options.text: Attach an SCP to account B that allows s3:GetObject for the IAM role of the application in account A on the bucket.
options.why: [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), so an SCP does not give the role access to the bucket.

items.explanation: The role and the bucket are in different accounts. AWS [allows the request only if both evaluations return Allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies). So account B allows the role in the bucket policy, and account A allows the action in the role's own policy. Both statements name one role and one action, so the bucket stays private.
items.takeaway: Cross-account access needs an allow in the resource's account and in the principal's account.
items.twin: If the stem said "a bucket in account A" instead: one statement is enough, because [the permissions of identity-based and resource-based policies are a union](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-same-account-identity-or-resource-allow).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for a combination of two steps that is MOST secure.
I mark the constraints: the role is in account A, the bucket is in account B, the bucket stays private, and only this application reads it.
Before I look at the options, I predict one step: a bucket policy in account B that names the role, because a bucket policy names who can read.
I remove the wildcard principal, because it makes the bucket public. I remove the SCP, because an SCP never grants permissions. I remove the IAM user, because its key is a long-term credential.

Between the bucket policy alone and the bucket policy with the role's own allow, the difference is the second account. My first idea breaks because the role and the bucket are in different accounts, so both accounts must allow the read; the bucket is in account B and the role is in account A, so I also choose the identity-based policy of the role.
Check: the two statements name one role and one action, and the bucket stays private. Time: 90 seconds.

items.stem: A company runs an order-processing application on servers in the company's data center. The application reads and writes objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. Company policy requires that no long-term credentials are stored where the application runs. The company also runs a private certificate authority that issues certificates to its servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: servers in the company's data center

options.text: Attach an IAM role through an instance profile, and let the AWS SDK load the temporary credentials from the instance metadata.
options.why: Instance profiles and instance metadata belong to Amazon EC2 instances. Servers in a data center are not EC2 instances, so no credentials arrive.
options.misconception: believes that an instance profile works for servers outside Amazon EC2

options.text: Use IAM Roles Anywhere with certificates from the private certificate authority, and exchange each certificate for temporary role credentials.
options.why: IAM Roles Anywhere [extends the capabilities of IAM to on-premises and hybrid cloud workloads](../facts/iam.md#iam-roles-anywhere-for-on-premises-and-hybrid-workloads), and the company already has the certificate authority.

options.text: Create an IAM user for the application, store its access key in an encrypted file where the application runs, and rotate it monthly.
options.why: Access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), so a stored key breaks the company policy, even when it is encrypted.

options.text: Move the application to new Amazon EC2 instances, and attach an IAM role to the new instances through an instance profile.
options.why: It works, but a migration to Amazon EC2 is far more work than using the certificate authority that the company already runs.
options.misconception: moves a workload to solve a credentials problem

items.explanation: The servers are outside AWS, so the instance profile path does not exist for them. Workloads outside AWS [can still use temporary credentials](../facts/iam.md#iam-best-practice-workloads-outside-aws-temporary-credentials), and IAM Roles Anywhere delivers them in exchange for a certificate. No key is stored, and the company already runs the certificate authority.
items.takeaway: Servers outside AWS get role credentials through IAM Roles Anywhere and a certificate.
items.twin: If the stem said "Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region" instead: an IAM role through an instance profile, because [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed).

items.stem: A company has an IAM role in its production account for reading reports from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same account. Developers in the company's development account must use the role. Their IAM policies allow sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN. When a developer calls AssumeRole, the call succeeds, but the next call to read a report fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the next call to read a report fails

options.text: Update the trust policy of the role in the production account so that it names the development account as a principal.
options.why: AssumeRole already succeeds, so the trust policy works. The failure comes later, inside the role session.

options.text: Update the permissions policy of the role so that it allows s3:GetObject on the report bucket and on the objects in it.
options.why: [The permissions policy of the role being assumed determines what the temporary credentials](../facts/iam.md#iam-role-permissions-policy-defines-session-permissions) can do, and the read is missing there.

options.text: Add a bucket policy to the report bucket that allows s3:GetObject for the development account as the principal.
options.why: Inside the session the caller is the role, not the developer, because [the permissions are not cumulative](../facts/iam.md#iam-assume-role-replaces-original-permissions).

options.text: Create an IAM user in the production account for each developer, with an access key and read access to the bucket.
options.why: It works, but each user brings long-term keys that [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), which is more work and more risk.
options.misconception: replaces a role with long-term keys

items.explanation: AssumeRole succeeds, so the trust check passed. The read fails inside the session, and [the permissions policy of the role being assumed determines what the temporary credentials](../facts/iam.md#iam-role-permissions-policy-defines-session-permissions) can do. Adding s3:GetObject to the permissions policy of the role fixes the session with one change.
items.takeaway: The session fails after AssumeRole succeeds: fix the permissions policy of the role.
items.twin: If the stem said "the call fails with an access denied error" instead: update the trust policy, because the request stops at the trust check.

items.stem: A company stores reports in an Amazon S3 bucket. Analysts sign in to the same AWS account and belong to an IAM group named analysts. A developer adds a statement to the bucket policy that names the ARN of the analysts group as the principal and allows s3:GetObject on the report objects. The statement does not give the analysts access to the reports. What should the developer name as the principal instead?
keywords: names the ARN of the analysts group as the principal

options.text: An IAM role that the analysts assume
options.why: A bucket policy can name a role: [you must indicate the account, user, role, or AWS STS federated user principal](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-element-resource-policy-not-identity-policy).

options.text: The name of the analysts group instead of its ARN
options.why: The form of the name changes nothing, because you [cannot identify a user group as a principal](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-group-cannot-be-principal).

options.text: A permissions boundary that is set on the analysts group
options.why: A boundary is not a principal, and it [does not provide permissions on its own](../facts/iam.md#iam-boundary-limits-but-never-grants).

options.text: The access key ID of each analyst's IAM user
options.why: An access key ID is a credential, not a principal: [you must indicate the account, user, role, or AWS STS federated user principal](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-element-resource-policy-not-identity-policy).
options.misconception: confuses a credential with the principal that holds it

items.explanation: In a bucket policy, [you must indicate the account, user, role, or AWS STS federated user principal](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-element-resource-policy-not-identity-policy), and you [cannot identify a user group as a principal](../facts/iam.md#iam-principal-group-cannot-be-principal). A role that the analysts assume is a valid principal. In one account, [the permissions of identity-based and resource-based policies are a union](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-same-account-identity-or-resource-allow), so the bucket policy can give the role the read.
items.takeaway: A bucket policy names a role or a user as the principal, not an IAM group.
items.twin: If the stem said "the analysts sign in to another AWS account" instead: the role also needs its own allow, because the [identity-based policy in the trusted account must allow the access](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-cross-account-needs-both-policies).
